title: Stopping the Cause Didn't Stop the Outage: Slack's 2-22-22
summary: On February 22, 2022, Slack was down for hours: many people could not connect. Slack's team stopped the maintenance that had started the outage, and it changed nothing, because by then the system was breaking itself. The maintenance was a routine batched upgrade; each restart briefly dropped cache servers, replaced automatically with empty ones. Two batches had gone fine the week before, but the third ran at peak traffic, when enough of the cache was empty to expose an expensive query it normally hid. One common startup request, looking up who is in your group chats, was cheap only while cached. With the cache empty, it had to search the entire database at once. The overwhelmed database timed out those very requests, so the cache stayed empty and fed itself. Engineers, not the trigger, ended it. They capped how many apps could start at once, protecting connected users and letting the cache refill; when they raised that cap too far, the overload returned, so they climbed back more slowly. Finally they fixed the expensive request.
crux: This failure did not end when its cause did. Slack paused the upgrade early but by then, it made no difference. 'We were in a cascading failure state, and systems in a cascading failure state do not normally return to a stable state without a significant reduction in load or increase in capacity.' The loop that had replaced the trigger fed itself. A partly empty cache sent the startup request to every part of the database on every cache miss. The overloaded database timed out the very requests that would have refilled the cache, and the still-empty cache produced the next wave of misses. Recovery needed the very resource the broken state was destroying. This is a metastable failure, a term from a paper Slack cites: the system stays broken on its own, not because anything is still going wrong, but because the broken state keeps regenerating itself. The only way is to fix it from outside: shed load to drop below the tipping point, or add capacity. Slack shed load, and chose who: users whose app had not finished loading were kept out so connected users could keep working.
cruxSummary: Slack paused the trigger early, but by then the failure was sustaining itself.
tradeoffs: The defining property of this failure class is that removing the cause does not help. Pausing the Consul rollout early was the correct move and accomplished nothing, because the system had crossed into a state that regenerates itself. An empty cache drives database overload, the overload times out the refill queries, and the still-empty cache drives the next round. Response plans built around 'find the trigger and stop it' are not enough here. The trigger is already in the past; the loop is the thing you have to break.

A cache that makes your traffic servable is capacity, not just an optimization, and its warmth is a hard dependency. Slack's database could not serve the startup traffic once the cache lost a realistic share of its hits; the system's real capacity assumed the cache was full. Systems in this position need to treat a full cache like any other planned, budgeted resource: protected during maintenance, warmed before serving, and monitored as closely as any other critical part of the system.

Better automation can make the system worse without being wrong. Mcrib replaced departed cache nodes faster and more correctly than its predecessor, and that speed turned a slow rolling restart into cache servers being emptied and replaced very fast. Repair speed is not free: every automatic 'repair' that costs the system something (an emptied cache server, a wipe, a failover) needs to be paced or budgeted, or held back until it is certain, otherwise its very speed makes things worse in exactly the situation it was built for.

Data layouts carry hidden amplifiers that only fire when the cache goes cold. The expensive query was invisible for as long as the cache absorbed it: data that never changes, kept for a long time, near-perfect hit rates. It turned each cache miss into a query against every shard the moment the cache went cold. The audit that matters is the one Slack ran afterward: find every high-volume query whose cost is only acceptable because a cache is currently hiding it.

Escaping a self-sustaining failure means shedding load below the tipping point, and shedding is choosing. Throttling client boots was a priority decision stated plainly: not-yet-connected users were kept out so connected users kept working and the cache could refill. The return trip has its own discipline: raising the limit too far in one step brought the outage back, while small steps, watching useful throughput at each one, got them home. Near a tipping point, both directions are dangerous: shed too little and you stay down, restore too fast and you relapse.

Retries contributed even though they were done right. Slack's apps wait longer and longer between tries, plus a random extra bit (the textbook discipline), and the postmortem still lists automated retries among the loads that fed the failure. The reason: a client cannot tell a brief local glitch (retry right away) from global overload (ideally, go quiet). Correct behavior in each client summed to harmful behavior across the fleet. The honest conclusion is that careful retry behavior in each client reduces what retries add to a pileup, but cannot remove it.

patterns.note: Slack's database tier could not serve the startup traffic without the cache absorbing most of it. The cache was really planned capacity dressed up as a mere optimization, and its warmth was a hard dependency that the maintenance churned away. The pattern names the discipline for systems in that position: treat the hit rate as capacity, protect warmth during maintenance, and warm a cache before promoting it. It also means auditing for queries whose cost is only survivable while the cache is hiding it.

Here the pattern shows up by its absence. Mcrib replaced dropped cache servers faster and more correctly than the system it replaced, and Slack's own verdict is exact: 'its efficiency made the broader system behave in a less safe way.' Every automatic repair that costs something (an emptied cache server, a wipe) needs pacing or a budget, and Slack's follow-up changes to the Mcrib control loop add exactly that restraint.

Here the pattern shows up during the incident, not in the design. The client-boot throttle was an explicit priority call: users without a booted client were kept out so connected users kept working and the refill queries could land. Then came the return-trip discipline the class demands: raising the limit too far in one step brought the outage back, and small steps, watching useful throughput at each one, restored full service.

artifact.teaser: Roll the Consul upgrade in 25% steps and watch two of them get absorbed, then land the third at peak traffic and cross the tipping point. Pause the rollout and watch it change nothing: the outage now keeps itself going. Throttle new logins to get back under the tipping point, raise the limit too far once to see it relapse, fix the expensive query, and walk the system home in small steps.

figures.caption: Group-DM membership is stored by user, so finding a channel's members means checking every shard. Warm, this is hidden; as the cache empties, nearly every boot queries every shard and load climbs far faster than the miss rate.
figures.ariaLabel: A warm one-entry query scatters to every shard on a miss, so load climbs faster than the miss rate.

figures.caption: Recovery means dropping traffic below the tipping point, then climbing back carefully. Throttling new boots keeps not-yet-connected users out so connected ones keep working and the cache refills. Coming back, one too-large jump relapses; the safe path is small steps.
figures.ariaLabel: Throttling new boots drops load below the tipping point; the return climbs in small steps, a big jump relapses.

figures.eyebrow: STOPPING THE CAUSE DID NOT HELP
figures.caption: Once the system tipped, this loop kept it broken: an empty cache forces scatter queries that overload the database, which times out the refill queries, keeping the cache empty. Pausing the upgrade does not touch it; only shedding load does.
figures.ariaLabel: A self-feeding loop: empty cache, scatter queries, database overload, timed-out refills, cache stays empty; only shedding load breaks it.

figures.caption: Startup requests go through Mcrouter, which spreads them across the cache servers. Mcrib decides which servers are in use by watching Consul's live list, and swaps in an empty spare whenever one drops off, which kept happening during the upgrade.
figures.ariaLabel: Requests pass through Mcrouter to the cache servers; Mcrib watches Consul and swaps in an empty spare when one drops.
